item.title: 'We've got time': Trump now suggests Iran war will continue into 2027
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
U.S. President Donald Trump boards Air Force One at Joint Base Andrews, Md., on Nov. 16, 2026. —Win McNamee—Getty Images President Donald Trump suggested he is putting off any major decisions on Iran until 2027, amid reports that he’s considering renewed major operations in the war that continues despite repeated promises that it’ll end soon. Speaking to Reuters on whether new major strikes are possible—the U.S. has engaged in limited strikes on Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz—Trump, who was en route to Washington following his trip to China, said, “Well, I’ll talk to you about it after the beginning of the year.” He added: “We’ve got time.” Trump made similar comments in other interviews. “We’ll see what happens after January 1st," the U.S. President told Fox News in an interview that aired on Thursday, just before his summit with China’s Xi Jinping and Russia’s Vladimir Putin . He also told Axios in a phone call Thursday that he was “not rushing into any decision” on Iran. The President initially promised that the war with Iran would only take weeks, but it has dragged on to nearly nine months, though major hostilities have subsided. Trump has previously said that the war would end immediately after the Nov. 3 midterm elections , but the impasse between Iran and the U.S. remained. And in the past weeks, he’s alternated between publicly threatening Tehran and holding off on authorizing new strikes at the request of American allies in the Gulf . Israel has reportedly tried to convince Trump of a new joint strike. The New York Times reported that the U.S. President is considering a new round of extensive military strikes on Iran, after Tel Aviv warned of Tehran’s “success in rebuilding its missile and drone arsenals and advancing its chemical and biological weapons programs.” Benjamin Netanyahu, the Israeli Prime Minister whose premiership is in limbo , is reportedly pushing for a four- to seven-day airstrike campaign on Iran. Axios reported, citing unnamed sources , that the White House sought input from the Pentagon and intelligence experts on how Iran would respond to the strike scenarios prepared by the U.S. military. Axios also reported that any U.S. campaign would involve Israel and could include strikes on Iran’s nuclear facilities such as Pickaxe Mountain, energy and other infrastructure, and Iranian military and civilian leaders. The U.S. midterm elections, in which Democrats won control of Congress as the American public largely rebuked Trump and the Republican Party following their handling of the Iran war and the economic fallout it caused, could complicate decisionmaking. Before the Nov. 3 elections, Trump said that Iran was willing to strike a deal, but after the GOP’s stunning losses, which Iranian leaders celebrated , the Administration’s messaging pivoted to maintaining economic sanctions and the blockade on Iran. Vice President J.D. Vance has blamed the war for the GOP’s election losses, but still appeared to defend the President’s foreign policy on Iran . The Vice President earlier said there was no difference between the President and members of his Administration on the war, but as Vance voiced his misgivings, Trump ordered the Vice President to shift his focus away from Iran diplomatic negotiations and toward domestic policies. Trump has a small window to push through further military action against Iran before the newly elected Democrats take office in January. On Thursday, the GOP-led U.S. Senate rejected a measure aimed at curbing the war . Trump addresses reported ‘dirty bomb’ threat In the interview with Fox News, Trump said he thinks people should not be alarmed by reports of a planned “ dirty bomb ” attack on Washington, D.C. A dirty bomb combines conventional explosives like dynamite with radioactive material. “If it does happen, we wipe them out,” Trump said. Trump acknowledged , however, that intelligence indicated Tehran is potentially interested in biological weapons. “Iran is looking at gases, looking at bio, because we’ve shut them out with the nuclear,” he said, referring to the damage that the U.S. has claimed it dealt to Iran’s nuclear facilities . Iran’s foreign ministry refuted Trump’s recent statements. “The allegations keep changing, but the underlying narrative remains disturbingly familiar,” spokesperson Esmaeil Baqaei said in a post on X . “Once again, the world is apparently expected to suffer a bout of collective amnesia." Baqaei then referred to how the U.S. justified its invasion of Iraq in 2003, alleging that the government of the late Saddam Hussein was developing weapons of mass destruction, which subsequent investigations found to be untrue. “We find ourselves facing ominous new allegations,” Baqaei said, “and a narrative that appears to be following the same fraudulent script.” This article originally appeared on Time at https://time.com/article/2026/11/20/iran-war-trump-strikes-major-decision-january-2027/

item.title: A child support fight exposed a Trump adviser's $15 million income
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Jason Miller was tapped to be Donald Trump’s first White House communications director, but a scandal ended that job in December 2016 before it even began. Miller stayed loyal, advising Trump’s next two campaigns and regularly defending him on cable news shows. In 2023, Miller’s accountant put his total income at about $879,000. Then, Trump was elected president a second time. And Miller proceeded to make more money than he had in the previous seven years combined. Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post. For the 12 months that ended in September 2026, he put his income at about $15 million, nearly all of it revenue from his two firms, according to a sworn financial statement he filed in court. In that time, Miller was a registered foreign agent for the governments of India and Romania and was in talks to join Trump’s White House as an unpaid adviser and began appearing there regularly this summer. Miller’s consulting firm continued receiving payments - about $1.3 million from July through September, bank records show. The details - some of which have not been previously reported and were recently included in the filings of a long-running Miami court case - offer a rare look at how lucrative Trump’s return to power has been for one of his most loyal aides. And they show how much money can flow to a presidential adviser without ever appearing in public disclosures. It took a child support fight - with the campaign aide at the center of his 2016 scandal - to bring that into view. In a statement to The Washington Post, Miller said, “I take all ethics, lobbying registration, and financial disclosure obligations seriously and have complied with all applicable requirements.” He said he was under no obligation to discuss his financial records or his court case. Miller did not respond to detailed questions about his time in the White House, his work and specific payments, including what they were for. Testimony about Miller’s income during the trial this week was first shared on social media by Grant Stern, a Democratic activist and executive editor of Occupy Democrats, who has followed the case for years. Miller’s bank records filed publicly in court show large payments from the government of India, the hedge fund Bridgewater Associates, the media company formerly called Paramount Skydance and a Japanese conglomerate - along with millions of dollars from sources the records do not identify. His gross income had already begun to climb in 2024, while he worked on Trump’s campaign; his accountant put it at about $1.6 million that year. In the 12 months that ended in August 2025, it reached about $4 million. By this fall, Miller’s two firms - SHW Partners and a second company, Scipio Strategic, both of which he owns outright, according to his filing - had together brought in about $15 million over a year. Scipio, which took in $6.7 million of that, does not appear in any public lobbying or foreign-agent filings, so who paid it, and for what, is not publicly disclosed. Most senior White House officials must publicly disclose their finances. Miller was different. His public lobbying and foreign-agent filings - which, by law, cover only payments received for disclosable activity - account for about $2.4 million of his income over the past two years. On Nov. 3 - Election Day - Miller wrote in a sworn financial affidavit he filed in the case that he “is currently an unpaid special government employee.” Where the form asks for his pay rate, the filing says “unpaid employee.” Where the form asked for his employer, he wrote “the White House.” In an unsigned statement Thursday, the White House said: “Jason Miller was never an SGE [special government employee] at the WH. We have enjoyed many different thoughts and opinions throughout this administration and will continue to do so. Our campus remains open to friends old and new, from either side of the political spectrum.” The White House did not respond to further questions about what Miller’s role was. When asked about the White House’s statement, Miller said, “I never completed the formal onboarding process.” Had Miller become a special government employee, he would have been exempt from federal limits on outside income and employment that apply to most White House staff, according to the Office of Government Ethics. But conflict-of-interest law would have barred him from working on government matters affecting his own financial interests or those of his clients, unless he received a waiver, said Kathleen Clark, a law professor at Washington University in St. Louis who studies government ethics. She said his lack of official status meant he could operate without committing to follow rules. “What you are describing is someone who has not sworn allegiance to this country, who doesn’t even purport to act in the interest in the public and is allowed to go running roughshod around the White House,” she said. From scandal to the West Wing Few people have been as close to Trump’s political operation and for as long as Miller. He was the chief spokesman for Trump’s 2016 campaign, and after the election Trump named him White House communications director. But within days, Miller withdrew amid reports of his extramarital affair with A.J. Delgado, another campaign aide who gave birth to their son in 2017. He spent the next decade working his way back - as a senior adviser on Trump’s 2020 and 2024 campaigns, as chief executive of Gettr, the pro-Trump social media platform, and as a vocal Trump booster. Joining the campaign in 2020, he said he was “humbled by the opportunity for a second chance to serve President Trump.” This summer, Miller started showing up regularly at the White House. Delgado, meanwhile, has sought child support from him in court since 2017; the case had never gone to trial until this month. Ahead of that trial to set regular child support, she subpoenaed his financial records. The firms’ bank statements, filed as an exhibit in the case, identify many payers by name. But for some wire transfers, they show only a date and an amount. In a summary she filed with the court before the trial, Delgado identified the senders of those wires. In Florida family cases, parties must exchange financial records, and Delgado also subpoenaed Miller’s bank records; not all of those records were filed with the court. Her monthly totals closely track the income Miller reported under oath. Most of Miller’s income last year came through his lobbying firm, SHW Partners, according to his filings. Its clients have included India, as the country has negotiated for better trade terms, the hedge fund Bridgewater Associates and the public relations firm Teneo, bank records show. Some clients had business before the Trump administration. A foreign government, a hedge fund and a media giant In April 2025, SHW Partners signed a $150,000-per-month contract to provide “strategic counsel, tactical planning, and government relations assistance” for India, according to documents filed with the Justice Department. India paid the firm $900,000 in 2025 and $750,000 in 2026 before Miller stopped working for the country in June, the documents show. As part of his work for India, Miller met with U.S. administration officials including Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, then-White House chief of staff Susie Wiles and others. In January, Miller traveled with Bessent to Minneapolis for a speech by Bessent to the Economic Club of Minnesota. At the time, India was paying his firm $150,000 a month to lobby, and Miller listed Bessent among the officials he contacted on India’s behalf. Paramount Skydance, through a subsidiary called Viacom, paid Miller’s firm SHW $420,000 in March and June, bank records show. At the time, Paramount was seeking the Trump administration’s approval to acquire Warner Bros. Discovery. The Justice Department cleared the $111 billion deal on June 12, without major conditions - nine days after the last payment to SHW. When the deal closed in October, the newly formed company rebranded as Skydance. The trading firm Susquehanna International Group, co-founded by billionaire Republican donor Jeff Yass, paid SHW about $234,000 in 10 payments from April 2024 to February 2025, bank records show. Susquehanna is one of the largest investors in ByteDance, TikTok’s Chinese parent company. On his first day back in office in January 2025, Trump paused enforcement of a law that would have banned the app. Spokespeople for Skydance and Susquehanna declined requests for comment. Other large payments came by wire, and their senders are identified only in Delgado’s summary. She attributed about $1.5 million - most of it in installments of $120,000 - to the Brooklyn Nets. The team is owned by Joseph Tsai, a co-founder of Alibaba, a Chinese tech giant that the Pentagon added in June to its blacklist of companies it says aid China’s military. Alibaba has said there was no basis for its inclusion. The Lawfare Defense Fund, a nonprofit that has raised at least $36 million to help pay legal bills for people it considers unjustly targeted by the legal system, according to the New York Times, paid Miller’s firm more than $1.4 million in fees, according to Delgado’s summary - including $300,000 in late September. Miller told the Times in June that “any payment that my firm may have received from the Lawfare Defense Fund would have been for communications consulting services.” The group has not issued any public press releases. A second firm, and a $3.35 million wire Miller’s other firm, Scipio, which he started in 2025, received most of its money in a handful of large payments, bank records show. After June, when Miller was in talks to join the White House, it stopped receiving deposits entirely; the payments that followed went to SHW. In December 2025, Scipio received a $3.35 million wire transfer that Delgado identified as coming from Celebrus Investments Limited, an investment holding company registered in Mauritius, an island nation that is a hub for offshore finance. Miller registered in May to work for Romania’s presidential administration for a fee of $300,000 as part of a $3.4 million lobbying contract held by the law firm Eversheds Sutherland, aimed at swaying U.S. energy investments, economic development and U.S.-Romania military cooperation. Bank records show that Eversheds paid Miller’s firms $2.45 million, starting about five months before he registered. The records do not say what the payments were for, and it is not clear whether they were related to the Romania work. In April this year, Scipio received a $100,000 transfer from a sender Delgado identified as Semafor, a week after the news media company hosted its World Economy 2026 summit in Washington. In an unnamed statement, a spokesperson for Semafor confirmed the payment to Miller’s firm Scipio and said it was for consulting services related to guest bookings at events. It’s a practice the company does with consultants from both sides of the aisle, the spokesperson said . The spokesperson also said that Semafor no longer has a relationship with Miller’s firm. Three corporate clients - Divergent Technologies, Mesabi Metallics and OKBL USA Holding - paid SHW about $700,000 in total to lobby for them in 2025 and 2026, federal lobbying filings show, and the bank records match. But OKBL also paid Scipio $500,000, in January and June. Because Scipio is not registered to lobby, that money does not appear in the filings; the records do not say what it was for. Representatives from India and Romania, as well as Mesabi, Eversheds, the Brooklyn Nets, the Lawfare Defense Fund, Teneo, Celebrus and Divergent did not respond to requests for comment. OKBL declined to comment. From inside the White House Even before this summer, Miller appeared at events and alongside Cabinet members and other advisers. In September last year, he committed to contribute $300,000 to Trump’s White House ballroom project, The Washington Post previously reported, and attended a dinner at the White House a month later for nearly 130 donors to the project. The Post reported in late June that the White House was in talks to bring Miller on to help with its messaging ahead of the midterm elections. By late July, he was photographed in the Oval Office. The payments continued. In the first days of July, SHW received $300,000 from Eversheds and $75,000 from Teneo; later that month came $75,000 from Bridgewater. On Aug. 18, a $450,000 deposit arrived with no payer listed. Delgado wrote in her summary that Miller testified in a Nov. 9 deposition that he did not know its source. In late September came two wires, for $300,000 and $120,000, that she attributed to the Lawfare Defense Fund and the Nets. A Bridgewater spokesperson said that Miller’s firm provided “strategic advice to the firm” but “that engagement was proactively paused when the firm learned that Mr. Miller was considering a formal government role.” Miller’s registration as an agent of Romania remained active until Aug. 4, and SHW reported lobbying for three corporate clients through July 31. By the fall, Miller was appearing at key moments alongside the administration’s most senior officials. Last month, Miller reportedly interrupted an interview that Katie Zacharia, the new press secretary, was giving the Wall Street Journal in her West Wing office, telling her that Vice President JD Vance wanted to speak with them. She did not return to the interview, and her time as press secretary soon ended, the Journal reported. In late October, Miller was part of a small group that helped secure a charter jet to fly Flávio Bolsonaro - a Brazilian senator and the son of former president Jair Bolsonaro - from Argentina to Miami after he lost Brazil’s presidential runoff election, the Wall Street Journal reported. Brazil’s Supreme Court had barred Bolsonaro from leaving the country. Trump has said he can stay in the United States “as long as he likes.” The bank records reviewed by The Post do not show payments from the Bolsonaro family. Beyond the Florida child support case, Delgado has also sued Miller in New York, accusing him of sexual assault. Miller has denied the allegations. This week, Miller agreed to pay Delgado $22,000 a month in child support, reaching a settlement in the Florida case after years of fighting that has spilled into public view. item.title: GOP leaders criticize members who are no-shows in Washington after losing re-election
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Speaker of the House Mike Johnson, talks with reporters in the US Capitol on Thursday, November 19. - Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc/Getty Images In one of Republicans’ final weeks in power, GOP leaders couldn’t convince enough of their members to come back to Washington to actually vote on their own bills — and Rep. Greg Murphy was furious. Murphy, who just lost his eastern North Carolina seat in one of the biggest upsets of the midterms, unleashed on his GOP colleagues in a closed-door meeting Wednesday, urging leadership to cut off pay for any lawmakers who don’t show up, according to multiple people in the room. “Look, I lost. I’m still here. I’m still here,” Murphy later told CNN about his frustrations at some of his colleagues’ delinquency. “If they aren’t here, they shouldn’t get paid.” After their historic midterm rout, Republicans are increasingly exasperated at their otherwise-healthy GOP colleagues who are refusing to come back to Washington after their election defeats. Speaker Mike Johnson and his GOP leadership team have been privately reprimanding those who chose not to come back, including one member who told the speaker they did not return because they were worried about a CNN report of the prospect of an Iranian “dirty bomb” plot in Washington. (Johnson, when learning of the reason for the member’s absence, reminded the member that their staff was in Washington working, according to a person familiar with the discussions.) “Attendance is a great frustration for me right now,” Johnson said Thursday. “We had 14 absences yesterday, so it’s not possible for us to advance a rule and advance our legislative agenda unless the members are here doing their job. … We want to run through the tape and finish strong, but we can’t do that unless people are present at work.” It’s a glaring — and familiar — problem for Hill GOP leaders, who struggled all year trying to keep a record-small majority in line. And it comes as Republicans were already struggling with how to achieve as much of President Donald Trump’s agenda as possible before being pushed deep into the minority in January. Republican leaders are under pressure to replenish Pentagon funding after months of war with Iran, but they don’t have the votes. They want to use their GOP trifecta to raise the debt limit to avoid a Democratic showdown with Trump next year. And they want to accomplish big legacy items, like permitting reform, before they’re forced to start over with Democrats in charge. House Republicans believe the best way to accomplish Trump’s wants — particularly on the debt limit and Pentagon funding for the war — is by sidestepping Democrats altogether and doing a party-line bill. But any party-line bill is logistically challenging in the Senate, where Majority Leader John Thune has put a pause on his party’s push to take that route. Now, Hill Republicans are increasingly worried they could squander their final days in power, with absences further complicating an already-difficult December puzzle. Some in GOP leadership privately fear that the only things Republicans will accomplish in December is punting government funding into the new year – maybe paired with an extension of the nation’s expired spy powers, according to multiple people familiar with the discussions. They also worry about political theatre that could distract from the agenda, with GOP Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky, a frequent leadership antagonist, forcing votes on the Epstein files and ending the Iran war. item.title: Iowans say warning Army is going to blow up degraded lead came too late
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Eight months after discovering a cache of highly reactive lead waste at an ammunitions plant in southeastern Iowa, the U.S. Army plans to do what it says is the only safe option: blow up the barrels. The controlled detonation of degraded lead azide was originally planned for Friday but was pushed to Monday after an outcry from residents and officials, who said they had not been given sufficient warning or input. Though the operation had been in the works for months, it wasn’t until Sunday that the Army notified the public about a resulting plume of lead particles that could extend as far as 100 miles north of the plant. In a Thursday night post on X announcing the delay, acting secretary of the Army Adam Telle said the three-day delay was the latest the explosion could be postponed before a forecasted cold snap, which would further destabilize the sensitive material. Get Climate Coach newsletter News and guidance on climate, science and technology. Sign up for free Shortly afterward, Sen. Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa) posted that the delay would allow the Army to “further educate the public.” But the extra time may not be enough to allay fears of lead contamination in a state where many are already on edge about the nation’s fast-rising cancer rate and potential health effects from pesticide use . Lead is a potent neurotoxin that can cause developmental problems and other health harms if it is inhaled or swallowed, according to the Environmental Protection Agency. Infants, children and pregnant women are especially vulnerable, and science has not established any safe level of exposure . “I understand that it is confusing and obviously this is not something that we wanted to do,” said Army spokeswoman Justine Barati. “But this is a emergent hazard that has to be addressed.” The degraded lead azide, an explosive used in munitions, has become so unstable it has to be destroyed, she said. Officials plan to detonate 68 barrels of the material inside the underground concrete chambers where they have been stored for 20 years. The buried chambers will be covered in two-stories worth of sand and sprayed down with misters in an effort to limit the amount of lead that is released. In an assessment released Wednesday, the Army concluded these measures will ensure the operation has a “less-than-significant impact” on the environment and public health. The Army posted an advisory this week instructing people to stay indoors with windows closed while the lead is airborne, and to wipe down surfaces that children might touch after the all-clear has been given. In Middletown, a 363-person town immediately next to the plant, some residents were told to evacuate in case the explosion causes windows to shatter. Yet many Iowans felt the communications around the detonation were too vague and came far too late. Even Iowa Gov. Kim Reynolds (R) found out about the operation from a public advisory just four days before the Army originally scheduled the operation, a spokesperson said. “It feels very rushed and very short term,” said one nearby resident, who spoke on the condition of anonymity for fear of backlash and because her relative works for the plant. “We’re all like, ‘Okay you’re saying this, but is it true, or how much of it is true?’” After learning the operation had been postponed, she said it was a “great sign” the Army was listening to residents’ concerns. Yet she and her family plan to leave the area on Monday, and she remains worried about what they will return to. Will her garden be contaminated? Will food grown in the surrounding farmland be safe to eat? Environmental groups on Thursday filed a lawsuit seeking an emergency stay of the detonation and a court review of the EPA’s decision to issue a permit. Several Iowa officials, including Gov.-elect Rob Sand (D) and U.S. Sen.-elect Josh Turek (D) also called on the Army to delay the operation until residents’ fears could be addressed. Representatives for Sand, Turek and the groups behind the lawsuit did not immediately respond to a request for comment about the Army’s decision to postpone. Under the terms of the EPA emergency permit , the Iowa Army Ammunitions Plant was required to map where airborne lead concentrations could reach 18 micrograms per cubic meter — a threshold below the federal exposure limit for workplace air. A second required map showed where the plume could deposit lead dust at concentrations of 5 micrograms per square foot (which the EPA considers a hazardous level of lead on floors ) and 100 micrograms per square foot (the hazardous level for window troughs ). These maps , released Sunday, showed that surface deposition of lead could extend 30 miles north, reaching the Mississippi River and parts of Illinois. Neither the Army nor the EPA responded to questions about what the maximum concentrations of lead in the plume are expected to be. Officials first became aware there was a problem during a regular inspection of the lead azide barrels at the plant this spring, Barati said. The liquid used to stabilize the material had dried out, and the lead azide began to form crystals — a condition that makes it much more likely to spontaneously explode. The Army is still trying to determine what caused the substance to recrystallize, Barati said. Most Read From The Washington Post A child support fight exposed a Trump adviser’s $15 million income The outages keep coming. Some Americans are preparing for a collapse. Just one minute of this activity may cut blood sugar spikes by 40 percent At historic summit, Xi and Putin share global stage with weakened Trump The 41 definitive rules of hosting A team of experts then spent the next several months trying to figure out what to do about it. Chemical neutralization would involve opening the barrels, potentially disturbing the crystals and creating “an extreme and unacceptable risk of fatal accidental detonation,” according to an Army assessment . Moving the barrels, either to an uninhabited area or even a more remote part of the facility, carried the same danger. If they did nothing, the lead azide would be a ticking time bomb — one that cold weather could make even more dangerous. By September, the Army concluded that a controlled detonation was the only viable option. The Army informed Middletown emergency services officials in September and held an open house for the town’s residents the following month, according to Barati. Communities beyond Middletown were not initially told about the operation because the lead levels they might be exposed to were thought to be “minuscule,” she said. But the EPA emergency permit, which was issued Nov. 13, required five day’s notice for anyone living within the plume, so the Army began reaching out to city councils, fire departments and other local officials, she said. By Monday, the news began trickling out on social media, raising alarm bells across the state. “When we first found out about it we thought it was fake,” said Cody Smith, a program manager for the Iowa Environmental Council. He said that local officials he spoke to had received no guidance from the Army or EPA on ways to protect their residents, and many were making decisions on the fly about whether to close schools and other facilities. The incident also raises questions about whether communities are safe from other hazards connected to the plant, Smith added. “Having not discovered this until earlier in the year is deeply concerning and speaks to a level of negligence from the Army itself,” he said. Barati said the Iowa plant was permitted to store lead azide and conducted inspections every six months to ensure it was safe. Some of the residents’ fear traces back to past concerns about the World War II-era facility, said Susan Dahl Mattoon, who grew up in the area and still works at Southeastern Community College in nearby Burlington. She recalled hearing the “booms” from ordnance tests and wondering what might be happening behind its gates. The plant was named a Superfund site in 1990 due to widespread soil and water contamination. About 10 years later, dozens of employees were found to have developed cancers likely related to their work on a nuclear weapons assembly line there. “Honestly our plant out here has had a reputation for looking the other way in the past,” Mattoon said. That’s why the short notice and lack of detail about effects has her so concerned, she said. David Cwiertny, director of the Center for Health Effects of Environmental Contamination at the University of Iowa, said it’s difficult to independently evaluate the possible risks from the detonation without additional information. The permit does not explain what models the Army used to forecast the potential lead dispersion or how they determined that the impact would be “less than significant.” The Army’s guidance for residents is also confusing, he said. If the level of lead in the plume is insignificant, why advise people to avoid the area and wipe down playground equipment afterward, he asked. If lead deposited on a slide is unsafe, why is it any better to wash it onto the ground where children might also be playing? Whether or not the detonation presents a major threat, the official messaging around it falls short of the central tenets of public health messaging, Cwiertny said. “Better engagement, better and clearer communication, focusing on what real public health risks are, explaining expertise and assumptions used to arrive at those conclusions — all of that is needed, else people are just going to fill in the blank with their own thoughts and frustrations,” he said. It tops off a turbulent week for the Department of Homeland Security , which oversees FEMA, following the potential cybersecurity concerns of last week’s air traffic control outage. “This closure is necessary to perform a comprehensive, building-wide pest control treatment to address an active pest issue and ensure a safe, healthy workspace for all personnel,” an internal memo to employees reportedly said, adding that staff would be updated once the situation had been “successfully resolved.” Employees at the Federal Emergency Management Agency’s Washington, DC, site have reportedly been ordered to stay home due to a bed bug infestation (AFP/Getty) The Independent has contacted FEMA for comment. Staff expressed frustration after Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin mobilized the agency after the nationwide ground stop on November 13. FEMA was instructed to coordinate with airports to help get medication and other supplies to stranded passengers across the country, but after 24 hours, the assignment ended. Staffers were reportedly “mostly sat around” with little to do. “It was a giant waste of time and resources,” a FEMA official told CNN. “Pull people from their actual important work to pretend they are doing work... and [potentially] infect them with bed bugs while doing it,” another staffer complained to the Post . Bed bug infestations can lead to people facing bites on their skin and unsanitary stains on their linens, plus time-consuming and costly efforts to find and eradicate the bugs. item.title: From MAGA stardom to a U-Haul: Lauren Boebert considers her own and GOP's losses
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Rep. Lauren Boebert sat in a U-Haul van in the nation’s capital after packing up her congressional office and her “dungeon of an apartment" on Thursday, about six years after she became a MAGA star and one week after voters decided not to return her to Washington, D.C. “I think about it every day," said Boebert, referring to the midterm elections where American voters sent Democrats to Congress en masse. Boebert spoke via Zoom from the van in one of her first interviews since her loss to Democrat Eileen Laubacher in a district Boebert had won by double digits two years ago. “This could be a referendum on President Trump. It could be the referendum on Congress or the Republican Party,” the Colorado Republican said. Then, lowering her voice, she added, “I think it’s all of it.” “I’m not mad at the president,” she said, but “the president did some things that hurt my voters.” Boebert was one of the most vocal and visible members of the “Make America Great Again” movement, making headlines with her right-wing righteousness on television and the House floor from the time she was first elected, in 2020. Her time in D.C. roughly traced the arc of that movement — and its supporters' more tenuous relationship with Trump of late — through its apogee in 2024 and its more recent midterm losses. As someone who described herself on Fox News as “ultra MAGA” four years ago, Boebert has become less inclined toward definitions. "When Jesus comes back and I’m raptured up, like all these labels are just going to fly off anyway," she said. “I respect President Trump, I still work with him, I want to continue to work with him. Not for him, with him.” Boebert says she hasn’t changed too much in her six years, besides a few more gray hairs and maybe some “personal growth” on bipartisanship. She said she wouldn’t have done anything differently — besides, she joked, “not gone to the theater.” She was referring to an incident at a Denver theater where she was caught on camera vaping at 2023 performance of "Beetlejuice" and escorted out of the venue, a clip that was replayed in campaign ads against her that she partly credits for her loss. She felt it was an unfair dredging up of a past she'd already “owned up to,” but said there could be “a great number of” unaffiliated or Republican voters who, when it came to the scandal, just said, “'I don't care if any of this is true or not, I'm tired of the drama.'” At the time, she apologized for it up and down her former district, which covered western Colorado. She later moved to a more conservative House seat covering the state’s Great Plains, where she won in 2024 before losing two years later. Boebert's opponent raised far more campaign cash than she did. “I didn’t raise millions of dollars and I kinda refused to,” she said. “Colorado voters know me, and, you know, if they know me enough to get rid of me, then I guess that’s my answer.” Though Boebert has broken from Trump at times — typically on topics other Trump supporters also opposed, such as the war in Iran and the administration's treatment of the Jeffrey Epstein files — she didn't lay the blame for her defeat or other GOP losses squarely at Trump's feet. “I think it’s more all of us. It’s all of the Republican Party,” she said, citing high gas prices, GOP infighting and unfulfilled promises. "We had solutions and we didn’t take action.” Boebert said she doesn't take her loss as an “L,” and instead sees it as a “launching pad” for the future, one that she didn't specify but gave a hint toward. “Too many people come to Congress and get rich,” she said. “I am not one of those, and I’m gonna go make some money now.” “The U-Haul is getting started,” she said, her camera vibrating a bit as the nation's capital outside the van's window started to move by. Employees have been told to return to work on staggered arrivals to avoid overloading the system with too many simultaneous logons, according to the source, but the expectation is that the majority of staff will be back to work by midday on Friday. “November 20, 2026, NSA Washington is operating under normal conditions with exceptions,” the voicemail said, detailing the staggering arrivals. “Personnel must follow their designating building opening times.” Several officials emphasized that the agency’s most sensitive and important intelligence gathering systems functioned throughout the outage. On several occasions over the past several days, some employees were told to report to work on a staggered basis, only have to return home without ever logging in, according to another source familiar with the agency’s response. The system, known as NSANet, has experienced outages before. But the length of the outage — almost four days — was unusually long and disruptive, current and former officials said. Multiple current US officials briefed on this week’s outage said it was not a cyberattack but instead appeared connected to the NSA’s handling of software updates for vulnerabilities in PHP, a programming language that powers about 70% of the world’s websites. item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Federal prosecutors announced charges against 14 people on Nov. 19 in connection with an alleged cargo theft ring accused of targeting at least three dozen trains in Southern California and stealing more than $22 million in merchandise, including Nike sneakers and Milwaukee tools. The Justice Department said the alleged ring targeted "high-value" trains traveling through Southern California that carried shoes, tools, and other products. The group allegedly coordinated the thefts via Instagram and sold the stolen goods on the black market. "The scale of the theft is staggering. We have charged a crew of 14 in a scheme to steal more than $22.5 million in cargo from at least three dozen freight trains in Southern California," said First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli in a released statement. "We will prosecute the people who raid these trains and those who knowingly turn stolen cargo into cash." According to the Justice Department, the ring operated from February 2024 to August 2026 and organized its thefts through Instagram messages. Prosecutors said Nathan Daniel Angel, 21, of East Los Angeles, led the ring. At least 36 trains were burglarized during the operation, the Justice Department said, with the group targeting trains carrying valuable merchandise that routinely arrives through the ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach, California. The burglaries occurred in Pico Rivera, Fullerton, and other locations in Southern California. Members of the alleged ring cut air hoses on the trains they targeted, forcing them to come to an emergency stop, prosecutors said. The stolen train cargo was later loaded into trucks and vans and transported to stash houses. According to prosecutors, members of the ring allegedly sold more than $1 million in stolen Nike sneakers and other merchandise to an unnamed Los Angeles-based sneaker and streetwear resale company in 2025. Others advertised the stolen merchandise on social media. Aged to steal? Company says $500K worth of bourbon stolen from depot Who was charged?
